        from pathlib import Path
        pages = {
        'concepts/01_forecasting_problem.md': '''# Traffic forecasting: what are we predicting?
        
        The task is to predict future traffic flow at 716 sensors using past observations.
        One example uses 12 historical readings and asks for 12 future readings at every
        sensor. With the assumed 15-minute cadence, that is three hours of history and
        three hours of forecasts.
        
        ```text
        Observed history → forecasting method → predictions → compare with actual future
        ```
        
        The target is the flow variable stored in the processed array. It is not speed.
        The file does not itself establish exact physical aggregation semantics.
        
        ## Time step, example, batch, and epoch
        
        - A time step contains all 716 sensors' readings at one array position.
        - An example pairs a 12-step input window with a 12-step target window.
        - A batch groups up to four examples for one model call.
        - An epoch visits every eligible training example once.
        - An optimizer update changes weights after one nonempty batch loss.
        
        With 21,001 training windows and batch size four, an epoch has 5,251 batches.
        The last has one example. Fifty epochs have 262,550 updates if no batch is skipped.
        
        ## Direct forecasts and rolling evaluation
        
        Our LSTMs output all 12 future steps together; they do not feed predictions back
        as inputs. At each later evaluation origin, actual observations available before
        that origin supply history. This is rolling-origin evaluation, not a single
        forecast of the entire test period.
        
        See [windows](05_sliding_windows.md), [batching](07_dataset_and_dataloader.md),
        and [the data implementation](../implementations/data_pipeline.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/02_arrays_and_tensor_shapes.md': '''# Arrays, tensors, indexing, and shapes
        
        NumPy arrays store the dataset. PyTorch tensors feed the model and support
        automatic differentiation and GPU execution.
        
        | Object | Shape | Axes |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | Source | `(35040,716,1)` | time, sensor, feature |
        | One history or target | `(12,716,1)` | window time, sensor, feature |
        | Batch | `(4,12,716,1)` | example, window time, sensor, feature |
        | LSTM sequences | `(4*716,12,F)` | sensor sequence, time, input features |
        
        `F=1` for the original LSTM; `F=41` for the contextual version.
        
        ## Python indexing
        
        ```python
        traffic[0, 0, 0]     # one scalar: first reading, first sensor
        traffic[:12, 0, 0]   # steps 0 through 11 for sensor 0
        traffic[0, :, 0]     # all sensors at step 0
        x[:, -1:, :, :]     # last input step, keeping a length-one time axis
        ```
        
        Indexing starts at zero. Slice endpoints are excluded. `:` selects a complete
        axis; `-1` selects its last entry. Keeping dimensions can make later broadcasting
        and repetition easier to understand.
        
        ## Reordering is different from reshaping
        
        For sensor-wise LSTMs, first reorder `(B,T,N,F)` to `(B,N,T,F)` with `permute`,
        then reshape to `(B*N,T,F)`. A direct reshape of the original layout would mix
        sensor and time positions. The output must reverse this organization.
        
        A raw NumPy slice can share memory with its source. Our constructed windows
        are new arrays, so editing a returned window does not edit source observations.
        Source data is float64. Model windows are float32; masks are boolean; calendar
        and sensor indices are int64. Small precision differences are normal when
        converting float64 values to float32 and reversing normalization.
        
        See [the contextual forward pass](../implementations/context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/03_data_quality_and_provenance.md': '''# Data quality, metadata, and provenance
        
        Good model scores require knowing what the input actually contains. Our files
        were copied from the previous project without alteration; hashes matched.
        
        `flowsd.npz` stores traffic; `sd_meta.csv` stores IDs, coordinates, and road fields.
        An SHA-256 hash fingerprints file bytes. A matching hash establishes identical
        bytes, not that the dataset's labels or provenance are correct.
        
        ## Checks and interpretation
        
        The audit found no nonfinite or negative readings, a range of 0–999, and
        563,841 zeros (2.2474%). Four consecutive frames, 6536–6539, are zero across
        all sensors. No sensor is zero for the entire array, but some are zero throughout
        individual splits. Four are zero throughout training.
        
        Metadata has 716 rows, unique ID/ID2 fields, valid coordinates, no duplicate
        coordinate pairs, and District 11 entries. These are structural checks.
        
        ## What remains assumed
        
        The NPZ has neither timestamps nor sensor IDs. We assume uninterrupted
        15-minute samples from January 1, 2019, and metadata-row/traffic-column pairing.
        Calendar plausibility does not independently prove timestamps or timezone.
        ID2 is a source-network index, not a direct index into the 716-column array.
        
        Zero readings may represent no traffic or missing data; we cannot recover the
        original validity flags. We preserve data and disclose the mask convention.
        Do not infer a cause for the all-zero interval from an assumed calendar label.
        
        See [audit implementation](../implementations/audit_data.md) and
        [observed audit report](../../reports/data_audit_v1/README.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/04_temporal_splits_and_leakage.md': '''# Chronological splits and information leakage
        
        Training estimates parameters. Validation selects configurations and checkpoints.
        Test assesses the frozen selected system. Their roles differ even when the same
        metric formula is used.
        
        | Split | Half-open interval | Frames |
        | --- | --- | ---: |
        | Training | `[0,21024)` | 21,024 |
        | Validation | `[21024,28032)` | 7,008 |
        | Test | `[28032,35040)` | 7,008 |
        
        A half-open interval includes its start and excludes its end. The first 60% is
        training, the final 20% test, and validation receives the rounding remainder.
        Time is split before constructing examples; dates are not randomly mixed.
        
        ## Leakage examples
        
        Fitting a scaler on all dates, deriving similarity from test traffic, selecting
        hidden width from test scores, or using target traffic in an input would leak
        information across the intended prediction boundary.
        
        Our scaler and seasonal table use training observations only. Every target
        window stays within one split. Earlier split observations may provide history:
        the first validation window uses the final training history. That history was
        already available at the forecast origin.
        
        Training-window shuffling does not reorder readings inside a window or move
        examples into another split.
        
        ## Reused test limitation
        
        The previous project tested this period, and the small LSTM was tested before
        the contextual redesign. Selecting contextual candidates on validation avoids
        additional direct test tuning, but does not make this test period newly unseen.
        The report must disclose that chronology and the follow-up nature of the study.
        
        See [experiment fairness](17_comparison_and_fairness.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/05_sliding_windows.md': '''# Sliding windows, history, horizon, and stride
        
        A model learns from input/target examples rather than one giant sequence.
        `target_start` is the first future index, not the first historical index.
        
        ```python
        past = values[target_start - history:target_start]
        future = values[target_start:target_start + horizon]
        ```
        
        For history/horizon 12 and `target_start=12`, input is `[0,12)` and target is
        `[12,24)`. At `target_start=13`, both move forward one step. Stride is one.
        
        ## Eligible origins
        
        ```python
        range(max(split_start, history), split_end - horizon + 1)
        ```
        
        The lower bound ensures enough history. The upper bound ensures every forecast
        target lies inside its split. The extra `+1` includes the last valid start because
        Python range excludes its stop.
        
        | Split | Windows | First target | Last target start |
        | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
        | Training | 21,001 | 12 | 21,012 |
        | Validation | 6,997 | 21,024 | 28,020 |
        | Test | 6,997 | 28,032 | 35,028 |
        
        Training count is `21024 - 12 - 12 + 1`. Validation/test can use earlier history,
        so each count is `7008 - 12 + 1`.
        
        Windows are built on demand; we do not allocate one expanded overlapping-window
        array. The underlying NPZ is still fully loaded into memory, not streamed from
        disk. Overlap also means one observed value can be scored at multiple forecast
        origins/leads; metric counts refer to forecast-target pairs.
        
        See [make_window and TrafficDataset](../implementations/data_pipeline.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/06_normalization_and_masks.md': '''# Normalization and zero-target masks
        
        These are separate rules: normalization controls input scale; the mask controls
        which future observations contribute to errors.
        
        ## One global training scale
        
        ```text
        z = (value - mean) / std
        value = z * std + mean
        ```
        
        The training mean is 247.19353447084683; population standard deviation is
        184.27468320611501. One pair is fitted across training frames and sensors,
        including zeros. Validation/test reuse it; no per-split refitting occurs.
        The value 29 becomes approximately -1.1841. A negative normalized reading simply
        lies below the mean; it does not mean negative traffic.
        
        Inputs become float32 after normalization. Targets remain in original units,
        also float32. Both LSTM classes inverse-normalize forecasts inside their forward
        pass, so predictions and targets are compared on the same original-unit scale.
        Inverse normalization remains differentiable.
        
        ## Mask policy
        
        ```python
        target_mask = y != 0
        ```
        
        True includes the target; False excludes it. Zero inputs are preserved and
        normalized, not filled. There is no imputation or interpolation.
        An all-masked training batch is skipped. An evaluation with no valid targets
        raises an error rather than reporting perfect accuracy.
        
        Zero exclusion follows the benchmark convention, not proven source validity.
        Seasonal averages exclude zero training readings, whereas the scaler includes
        them. These different rules are intentional. Scores can exclude whole sensors
        when their targets are all zero; report coverage with accuracy.
        
        See [metric implementation](../implementations/evaluation.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/07_dataset_and_dataloader.md': '''# Dataset and DataLoader
        
        A Dataset explains how to obtain one example. A DataLoader asks for examples,
        converts them to tensors, and groups them into batches.
        
        `TrafficDataset.__init__` stores array references, normalization, dimensions,
        and eligible starts. `__len__` reports windows. `__getitem__` creates one
        normalized `x`, original-unit `y`, boolean mask, and integer `target_start`.
        
        ```python
        loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=4, shuffle=True,
                            generator=generator, num_workers=0)
        ```
        
        Training is shuffled; validation is sequential. The seeded generator makes
        training order reproducible and its state is saved for resume. `num_workers=0`
        uses the current Python process, not background loading workers.
        
        ```python
        batch = next(iter(loader))
        ```
        
        `iter` creates a batch iterator; `next` gets one batch. For full batches:
        
        | Entry | Shape | Type |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | x | `(4,12,716,1)` | float32 |
        | y | `(4,12,716,1)` | float32 |
        | target_mask | `(4,12,716,1)` | bool |
        | target_start | `(4,)` | int64 |
        
        The Dataset does not currently return calendar features. Contextual model
        runners reconstruct historical calendar from `target_start`. There are 5,251
        training batches; the last has one example because `drop_last` remains False.
        Four windows contain 2,864 per-sensor sequences for a shared sensor-wise LSTM.
        
        Iterator creation can consume random-generator state. Correct resume therefore
        restores RNG state after model initialization and preserves it around probes.
        
        See [checkpoint/RNG concepts](13_checkpoints_and_resume.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/08_baselines.md': '''# Persistence and seasonal-average baselines
        
        A baseline is a simple reference predictor. A neural model is useful only in
        relation to meaningful alternatives, not merely because it has learned weights.
        
        ## Persistence
        
        Repeat each sensor's latest observed value for all 12 future steps. It learns
        nothing. If the last reading is 106, all 12 forecasts are 106. Our implementation
        extracts the last normalized input step, restores original units, and repeats it.
        
        This can work for slowly changing near-term traffic but cannot anticipate a
        change from the last level.
        
        ## Seasonal average
        
        Learn average nonzero training traffic for each weekday, 15-minute slot, and
        sensor. There are `7*96=672` calendar groups; table shape is `(672,716,1)`.
        Future calendar groups are known without observing future traffic.
        
        If a group's sensor mean has no observations, use that sensor's overall nonzero
        training mean. If the sensor is entirely zero during training, use the global
        nonzero training mean. An entirely zero training array cannot fit this baseline.
        
        The seasonal table is fitted once on training and is never updated on validation.
        It has no neural layers or optimizer, but it does estimate statistics.
        
        ## Observed validation reference
        
        | Metric | Persistence | Seasonal average |
        | --- | ---: | ---: |
        | MAE | 64.1336 | 19.7442 |
        | RMSE | 99.3846 | 36.4470 |
        | MAPE (%) | 41.5436 | 12.4536 |
        
        These are validation results. Do not compare them directly with a test score.
        They show that recurring temporal structure is a strong reference on this task;
        they do not establish why a neural model succeeds or fails.
        
        See [baseline code](../implementations/baselines.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/09_metrics_and_aggregation.md': '''# MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and correct aggregation
        
        Let `e = prediction - target` and let `K` be included forecast-target pairs:
        
        ```text
        MAE  = sum(abs(e)) / K
        RMSE = sqrt(sum(e²) / K)
        MAPE = 100 * sum(abs(e) / abs(target)) / K
        ```
        
        MAE measures average magnitude in traffic units. RMSE also uses traffic units
        but emphasizes large errors. MAPE expresses relative error as a percentage.
        For prediction 120 and target 100, absolute error is 20, squared error 400,
        and percentage error 20%.
        
        Zero targets are masked before division. There is no extra near-zero threshold
        or epsilon in our implementation; small nonzero targets can inflate MAPE.
        
        ## Why not average batch scores?
        
        A batch with 2 included targets and error sum 10 has MAE 5. Another with 6 targets
        and sum 18 has MAE 3. Correct pooled MAE is `(10+18)/(2+6)=3.5`, not 4.
        Accumulate sums/counts first, then calculate the metric. Likewise, overall RMSE
        comes from pooled squared errors, not a mean of per-batch or per-lead RMSEs.
        
        Our training score pools predictions produced by evolving weights. Validation
        uses one frozen set of weights. They are not two scores for the identical model
        state, even though they share formulas.
        
        ## Forecast leads and coverage
        
        Lead 1 is assumed 15 minutes ahead; lead 12 is 180 minutes. Per-lead metrics
        expose errors hidden by an overall score. The same physical reading can appear
        as different forecast-target pairs because origins overlap.
        Validation has 58,367,674 included pairs; test has 58,158,396 under this protocol.
        
        See [metric code](../implementations/evaluation.md) and
        [test scoring](../implementations/evaluate_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/10_lstm_gates_and_states.md': '''# How the LSTM processes history
        
        At time t, an LSTM combines the current feature vector x with its previous hidden
        state h and cell memory c. Gates are learned vectors, not hand-coded traffic rules.
        
        ```text
        f = sigmoid(Wf [x,h_previous] + bf)    # retain previous cell memory
         i = sigmoid(Wi [x,h_previous] + bi)  # admit candidate memory
         g = tanh(Wg [x,h_previous] + bg)     # propose candidate content
         o = sigmoid(Wo [x,h_previous] + bo)  # expose updated memory
         c = f * c_previous + i * g
         h = o * tanh(c)
        ```
        
        Here `*` is element-wise multiplication and `[x,h]` concatenates vectors.
        Sigmoid lies between zero and one; tanh between minus one and one. A forget
        component near 0.9 retains most of the corresponding old memory component.
        The equations summarize conceptual biases; PyTorch stores separate input and
        recurrent bias vectors for each gate.
        
        Hidden width is the number of components in h and c, not the number of sensors
        or forecast steps. These components have learned numerical meanings; we cannot
        assume one means morning traffic or another means congestion.
        
        ## One layer versus two
        
        The first layer processes chronological input features and outputs a hidden
        representation at every step. A second LSTM layer processes that sequence, not
        just its final state. Our head uses the last step's top-layer hidden output.
        
        Both implemented LSTMs begin each independent window with zero hidden/cell
        states. They do not carry state between shuffled windows. All 12 forecasts are
        produced together by a linear head; no future traffic is supplied.
        
        Shared parameters process every sensor. This is not 716 separately trained
        models, and it does not by itself provide communication between sensors.
        
        See [small LSTM](../implementations/lstm_model.md) and
        [contextual LSTM](../implementations/context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/11_embeddings_and_context.md': '''# Learned calendar and sensor embeddings
        
        An embedding is a trainable lookup table. Given an integer ID, it returns that
        row's vector. Training gradients update the relevant rows. The row is not a
        precomputed traffic measurement or a guaranteed interpretable feature.
        
        | Table | Rows | Vector width | Trainable values |
        | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
        | Time of day | 96 | 16 | 1,536 |
        | Weekday | 7 | 8 | 56 |
        | Sensor identity | 716 | 16 | 11,456 |
        
        At each historical step, concatenate 1 normalized traffic value, 16 slot values,
        8 weekday values, and 16 sensor values: 41 inputs. The sensor vector stays the
        same across that sensor's history. Calendar vectors follow the historical steps.
        
        ## Calendar reconstruction
        
        For absolute time index t:
        
        ```text
        slot = t % 96
        weekday = (1 + t // 96) % 7
        ```
        
        Monday is zero; the assumed January 1, 2019 start is Tuesday, so the offset is
        one. `%` wraps a cycle; `//` counts complete days. `input_calendar` constructs
        indices `target_start-12` through `target_start-1`, excluding the target start.
        Original timestamps/timezone remain unverified.
        
        ## Why context may help
        
        The same recent flow can imply different futures at different times or sensors.
        Context lets the shared model learn conditional patterns. Sensor identity is
        not coordinates or neighboring traffic; contextual LSTMs still process each
        sensor's sequence independently.
        
        We changed context, layers, and capacity together relative to the small LSTM.
        Their combined improvement cannot identify each factor's separate contribution.
        
        See [context model implementation](../implementations/context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/12_training_gradients_and_adam.md': '''# Training: loss, gradients, and Adam
        
        Training adjusts learned parameters using training examples. It does not adjust
        the fixed global normalization statistics.
        
        ```python
        model.train()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        prediction = model(inputs)
        loss = masked_mae(prediction, target, mask)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        ```
        
        `zero_grad` clears previous gradients because PyTorch otherwise accumulates them.
        The forward pass calculates predictions. Masked MAE gives one differentiable
        scalar. `backward` calculates gradients via the chain rule; it does not update
        weights. Adam's `step` uses gradients and running first/second-moment estimates
        to update parameters. Our learning rate is 0.001.
        
        ## What gets learned?
        
        Small LSTM: recurrent/input weights, biases, and linear head. Contextual LSTM:
        those parameters plus sensor and calendar embedding tables. The output's inverse
        normalization is differentiable, so original-unit loss still reaches all layers.
        
        All-masked batches are skipped; missing or nonfinite gradients and nonfinite
        weights stop training. Loss may rise between batches because the batches differ.
        A short diagnostic establishes usable gradients/updates, not generalization.
        
        ## Our fixed contextual protocol
        
        Two layers; widths 128/256/384; no dropout; Adam with no weight decay, scheduler,
        or clipping; batch size four; seed 2023; 50 epochs per candidate. Training shuffles
        windows and keeps their internal time order. The original PatchSTG used different
        optimizer settings, so equal epochs do not mean identical optimization.
        
        See [diagnostic](../implementations/train_lstm_diagnostic.md) and
        [candidate runner](../implementations/train_context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/13_checkpoints_and_resume.md': '''# Checkpoints, randomness, and resume
        
        A checkpoint is saved experiment state. `best.pt` serves model selection;
        `last.pt` serves continuation. They can refer to different epochs.
        
        Validation MAE chooses best. We use strict improvement, so an exact tie retains
        the earlier epoch. Restoring a model's weights alone is insufficient for the
        same Adam trajectory: optimizer moments and random-generator states matter too.
        
        The contextual runner's last checkpoint includes current weights, Adam state,
        CPU/CUDA RNG state, shuffle-generator state, epoch history, best model so far,
        and experiment metadata. Mean/std are fixed model buffers included in weights.
        
        ## Why restore RNG after initialization?
        
        Constructing layers consumes random numbers. Model construction must finish
        before restoring the saved RNG state. Shuffle uses a dedicated generator.
        CUDA RNG state and CPU generator state are stored separately; RNG tensors must
        be restored in the form expected by their respective APIs.
        
        ## Interruptions
        
        Saves occur at epoch boundaries. Stopping mid-epoch loses that partial epoch;
        resume repeats it from the previous completed checkpoint. The runner writes a
        temporary file before replacing `last.pt`, reducing exposure to partial saves.
        For the contextual suite, last owns best/history so derived files can be repaired.
        No design can guarantee recovery from storage corruption; preserve artifacts.
        
        Completed candidates are loaded and verified on resume, then the incomplete
        candidate continues. Source/data hashes, settings, device and recorded versions
        must match. Editing training code while a run is in progress can prevent resume.
        
        A saved seed is not a universal cross-device reproducibility guarantee.
        Deterministic operations and matching state help within a recorded environment.
        
        See [pause/resume commands](../commands.md) and
        [context training implementation](../implementations/train_context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/14_validation_selection_and_overfitting.md': '''# Validation selection and overfitting
        
        Training data changes parameters; validation guides model choices. Test scores
        must not choose hidden width, learning rate, epoch, or the next attempted variant.
        
        Our contextual study predefines widths 128, 256, and 384. Each trains 50 epochs.
        Within a candidate, select lowest full-validation MAE, keeping the earlier epoch
        on exact ties. Across candidates, select lowest best MAE; exact ties favor the
        smaller hidden width. Record all candidates, not only the winner.
        
        ## Reading learning curves
        
        Training loss pools evolving-model predictions; validation scores frozen weights.
        If training continues improving while validation worsens, this suggests
        overfitting or an optimization path that generalizes less well. One higher
        validation epoch is not proof; examine the curve and variation.
        
        The completed contextual 128/256 candidates had their best checkpoints before
        epoch 50. That is why best and last have distinct roles. A larger model is not
        guaranteed better validation performance.
        
        ## Diagnostics versus evidence
        
        A shape/gradient check says the computation works. A repeated-batch probe can
        show updates help that batch. Neither is a validation result. One seed does not
        show statistical significance; one network does not demonstrate scalability.
        
        The contextual redesign followed observed small-LSTM test results. We disclose
        this and select subsequent candidates on validation. A final contextual test
        pass has not yet occurred at the documented snapshot.
        
        See [results snapshot](../results_and_status.md) and
        [capacity experiment rules](../../LSTM_CAPACITY_EXPERIMENT.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/15_gpu_precision_and_timing.md': '''# GPU execution, precision, utilization, and timing
        
        A CUDA-enabled environment does not automatically put a model on the GPU.
        Weights, input tensors, targets, calendar, and masks must be on compatible
        devices. Restored Adam state must also match its parameters' device requirements.
        Our first LSTM epoch was CPU; later continuation used CUDA in the user's terminal.
        
        GPU utilization is sampled activity, not a direct measure of useful speed.
        Small kernels, CPU preparation, transfers, and synchronization can limit it.
        Compare epoch duration under documented settings rather than targeting 100%.
        
        ## Precision and the failed parity check
        
        An early contextual GPU probe passed width 128 but failed isolated-versus-batched
        agreement at width 256. Batched/sliced numerical kernels can differ. The agent's
        build had cuDNN RNN TF32 enabled by default; this was a possible contributor,
        not a proven diagnosis of the host failure.
        
        The contextual probe/trainer now explicitly sets global, matmul, and cuDNN RNN
        precision to IEEE FP32, with no AMP. Deterministic algorithms alone do not set
        these precision controls. The corrected GPU probe passed all three widths.
        It also checks actual recurrent inputs exactly, so layout correctness does not
        rely only on output tolerance. See the
        [recorded follow-up](../../LSTM_CAPACITY_EXPERIMENT.md).
        
        ## Timing scope
        
        CUDA runs asynchronously. The probe synchronizes before/after timed updates and
        excludes one warm-up update. It repeatedly uses an already transferred batch;
        its estimate omits full-epoch loading/validation. Training reports record real
        epoch times including checks and accumulation. These are not controlled
        cross-architecture speed benchmarks.
        
        The agent environment cannot currently access CUDA; the user's terminal can.
        CPU checks and host GPU evidence are identified separately in reports.
        
        See [GPU probe implementation](../implementations/check_context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/16_parameter_counts_and_capacity.md': '''# Parameters, hidden width, and capacity
        
        A trainable parameter is a learned scalar weight or bias. Input observations,
        hidden activations, Adam moments, and fixed mean/std buffers are not counted as
        trainable parameters. Sensor count increases computation; shared recurrent
        weights are not replicated into 716 separate models.
        
        For one PyTorch LSTM layer with input width d and hidden width h:
        
        ```text
        parameters = 4h(d + h + 2)
        ```
        
        There are four gate/candidate calculations, each using input/recurrent weights
        and two biases. A linear head from h to 12 adds `12h+12`.
        
        Small model: `4*32*(1+32+2) + 32*12+12 = 4,876`.
        
        Contextual model adds 13,048 embedding parameters and two recurrent layers:
        
        ```text
        13,048 + 4h(41+h+2) + 4h(h+h+2) + 12h+12
        = 12h² + 192h + 13,060
        ```
        
        | Hidden width | Parameters |
        | --- | ---: |
        | 128 | 234,244 |
        | 256 | 848,644 |
        | 384 | 1,856,260 |
        
        Earlier conversation estimates were approximate; these are exact code counts.
        Increasing hidden width has a roughly quadratic parameter cost and also increases
        activation memory and per-update work. It may improve representation, overfit,
        or simply require different optimization. Size alone is not accuracy.
        
        Previous PatchSTG has 2,284,844 parameters. Similar counts do not equate spatial
        information, architectures, or optimization budgets. Report all those differences.
        
        See [comparison fairness](17_comparison_and_fairness.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/17_comparison_and_fairness.md': '''# Comparing LSTM and PatchSTG responsibly
        
        Our active course project compares contextual temporal LSTM with a previous
        PatchSTG adaptation; BigST is deferred. LSTM directly applies the course method.
        
        ## Shared protocol
        
        The inspected previous PatchSTG records match the dataset hash, split boundaries,
        normalization, history/horizon 12, stride one, batch size four, masks and test
        coverage used by the LSTM. Both use 50 training epochs and validation-based
        checkpoint selection. These support a shared forecasting-task comparison.
        
        ## Remaining differences
        
        | Aspect | Contextual LSTM | Previous PatchSTG |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | Traffic history | Per-sensor | Across sensors through spatial attention |
        | Calendar and identity | Learned embeddings | Calendar projection/embeddings and sensor embeddings |
        | Coordinates/similarity | Not used | Organize/pad spatial patches |
        | Optimizer | Adam, fixed 0.001 | AdamW, initial 0.002, schedule/decay/clipping |
        | Search budget here | Three widths | Existing configured run |
        | Parameters | 234k–1.856m | 2.285m |
        
        The old small traffic-only LSTM was an especially unequal capacity/context
        comparison. The new model is a stronger reference, but the comparison still does
        not isolate architecture alone. Matching epoch count aligns dataset passes,
        not total computation or tuning effort.
        
        We can claim which documented system performs better on matching validation/test
        windows. We cannot attribute a difference solely to spatial attention without
        controlled ablations, or claim statistical significance from one seed.
        
        ## Interpretation plan
        
        Examine per-lead errors, predefined traffic/time conditions, sensor-level errors,
        coverage, parameters and consistently measured costs. State hypotheses as such.
        Pick subgroup rules using training/validation rather than looking for favorable
        test examples. PatchSTG is not guaranteed to beat LSTM.
        
        The previous project is a code-aligned shared-protocol adaptation, not an official
        full-paper reproduction. It has not been reimplemented in this new folder.
        See [PatchSTG reference](../patchstg_reference.md).
        ''',
        'concepts/18_frozen_test_evaluation.md': '''# Frozen test evaluation
        
        After all model/epoch choices are fixed using validation, score the selected
        checkpoint on the held-out test period without changing parameters. This is
        assessment, not a training stage.
        
        Our small LSTM was selected at epoch 49. Its evaluator confirms training source
        and data hashes, scaler and splits, completed-run selection metadata, and
        validation reproduction before scoring test. Evaluation uses model.eval() and
        no gradient tracking. No optimizer is constructed.
        
        The evaluator records aggregate and 12 per-horizon metrics. It checks source
        mask counts, unchanged model state and unchanged checkpoint hash. CPU evaluation
        followed GPU training, with a validation tolerance guarding small device rounding
        differences. The device and tolerance must be disclosed.
        
        The small LSTM test MAE is 39.7079. Contextual models are different architectures
        and have a different checkpoint schema: evaluate_lstm.py cannot be used directly
        on their best.pt files. A separate explained evaluator is still needed after
        contextual candidate selection.
        
        ## What to do after seeing test scores
        
        Keep results fixed. Do not use a poor horizon or overall score to choose a new
        hidden width, scheduler or checkpoint and call the same test period unseen.
        If additional follow-ups are undertaken, disclose the chronology and limitation.
        
        See [small-model evaluator](../implementations/evaluate_lstm.md) and
        [results/status](../results_and_status.md).
        '''
        }
        for name, content in pages.items():
         p=Path('docs')/name; p.write_text(content)
        print('Wrote',len(pages),'concept guides.')
        PY

        'data_pipeline.md':'''# Implementation: data_pipeline.py
        
        Source: [data_pipeline.py](../../data_pipeline.py).
        
        This module provides reusable preparation functions. Importing it does not load
        the dataset or run evaluations.
        
        ## Functions in reading order
        
        1. `load_traffic(path)` opens NPZ with `allow_pickle=False`, extracts `data`, and
           closes the archive. The returned array stays in memory. This minimal loader
           does not itself enforce dataset shape/value/metadata checks; the audit does.
        2. `split_boundaries(total_steps)` calculates training end at 60% and test start
           before the final 20%. Validation receives the remainder.
        3. `fit_normalization(training_values)` computes one float64 mean/population std,
           including zeros. It rejects invalid statistics or nonpositive std. The caller
           must pass training observations only.
        4. `make_calendar_keys` maps assumed chronological indices to weekday/slot groups
           for the seasonal baseline. It returns keys, not source timestamps.
        5. `make_window` selects past/future, normalizes past, casts copies to float32,
           and returns x, original-unit y, and `y != 0` mask. It checks window bounds.
        6. `TrafficDataset` stores references/settings and a range of eligible starts.
           `__len__` counts starts; `__getitem__` calls make_window and adds target_start.
        
        ## Contract
        
        One example has x/y/mask `(12,716,1)`; a DataLoader adds the batch dimension.
        The calendar is not currently part of Dataset output. Contextual runners derive
        it from target_start, avoiding a change to this original module during training.
        All split datasets share the underlying traffic array and training scale.
        
        ## Verification and practical limits
        
        The walkthrough checks first/last source correspondence, all split target bounds,
        normalization reversal and independent window storage. The audit handles richer
        source validation. This is intentionally small educational infrastructure,
        not a generalized production loader for arbitrary datasets and cadences.
        
        See [splits](../concepts/04_temporal_splits_and_leakage.md),
        [windows](../concepts/05_sliding_windows.md), and
        [normalization/masks](../concepts/06_normalization_and_masks.md).
        ''',
        'inspect_data.md':'''# Implementation: inspect_data.py
        
        Source: [inspect_data.py](../../inspect_data.py).
        
        This is the executable learning walkthrough. `main()` calls imported preparation,
        baseline and evaluation functions, prints examples, and runs inline checks.
        The main guard prevents loading or evaluation when another module imports it.
        
        ## What happens when run
        
        1. Resolve local data relative to the script and load traffic.
        2. Print shape, dtype, first sensor readings, split boundaries and slice shapes.
        3. Fit training normalization and demonstrate inverse recovery.
        4. Construct/inspect split windows and verify eligibility/source correspondence.
        5. Build Datasets and a sequential first training batch for inspection.
        6. Demonstrate persistence and masked MAE on that batch.
        7. Evaluate persistence on full validation and independently recompute raw scores.
        8. Fit seasonal averages and exercise synthetic fallback examples.
        9. Evaluate seasonal average on the same validation windows and check counts.
        
        ```bash
        python inspect_data.py
        ```
        
        No neural training, checkpoint saving, or test prediction evaluation occurs.
        Despite its name, it now includes preprocessing and baseline demonstrations,
        not just file inspection. The separate audit handles source quality/plots.
        
        ## Checks to understand
        
        Source and inverse-scale checks guard wrong slices/units. Batch checks guard
        collation/layout errors. Raw persistence recomputation bypasses model batching
        and normalization. Synthetic examples check zero-mask MAE and seasonal fallback.
        Assertions are educational checks; running Python with -O disables assertions.
        There is no large formal pytest suite in this new implementation.
        
        See [data pipeline](data_pipeline.md), [baselines](baselines.md), and
        [evaluation](evaluation.md).
        ''',
        'audit_data.md':'''# Implementation: audit_data.py
        
        Source: [audit_data.py](../../audit_data.py).
        
        `main()` hashes the local files, loads traffic, calls audit_values and
        audit_metadata, and saves training-only plots with Matplotlib's Agg backend.

        ## Functions
        
        - `audit_values`: expected shape, real numeric dtype, finite/nonnegative values,

          ID/ID2, finite legal coordinates, District 11, and duplicate-coordinate count.
          It preserves row order and does not claim to prove column pairing.
        - `plot_patterns`: fixed sensor positions 0/358/715 for first-week histories,

        ''',
        'baselines.md':'''# Implementation: baselines.py
        
        Source: [baselines.py](../../baselines.py).
        
        ## persistence_forecast
        
        Input: normalized x `(B,12,N,1)`, mean/std, horizon. It selects `x[:,-1:,:,:]`,
        converts to float64, reverses normalization, and repeats across the time axis.
        Output is `(B,horizon,N,1)` in original traffic units. Reversing float32 input
        normalization can produce tiny differences from the raw integer-valued readings.
        There are no learned parameters or optimizer.
        
        ## fit_seasonal_average
        
        Input: training traffic and aligned calendar keys. It counts nonzero observations,
        calculates the global nonzero mean, then sensor nonzero means. The initial
        `(672,N,1)` table repeats sensor means as fallback. For each weekday/slot key,
        it replaces positions with group means where group counts are nonzero.
        
        `np.divide(..., out=..., where=...)` avoids dividing by zero and retains fallback
        values where no group observations exist. A sensor with no nonzero training
        readings uses the global mean. Entirely zero training input raises an error.
        
        The function returns a lookup table, not an object with a prediction method.
        `evaluate_seasonal` indexes that table using the future forecast calendar keys.
        The runner is responsible for training-only fitting and valid aligned inputs.
        
        ## Verification
        
        Persistence is compared with last raw source readings. A small two-sensor example
        checks weekday/slot averaging and both seasonal fallback levels. Full validation
        counts match between the two baselines; persistence also has an independent
        full raw-array metric calculation.
        
        See [baseline concepts](../concepts/08_baselines.md) and
        [evaluation implementation](evaluation.md).
        ''',
        'evaluation.md':'''# Implementation: evaluation.py
        
        Source: [evaluation.py](../../evaluation.py).
        
        ## masked_mae(prediction, target, mask)
        
        Checks matching shapes, boolean masks, finite predictions/targets, and at least
        one included target. It returns the mean absolute error after boolean indexing.
        This scalar retains gradients when called during training; it is not detached.
        
        ## evaluate_persistence
        
        Runs the persistence rule under `torch.no_grad()`. Across loader batches it
        accumulates absolute errors, squared errors, relative errors, target count, and
        window count. It calculates pooled metrics at the end and returns a metric
        dictionary plus valid-count/window-count values. An empty evaluation fails.
        
        ## evaluate_seasonal
        
        For each example, adds `[0,...,11]` to target_start, maps those future indices
        to calendar keys, and indexes the already fitted seasonal table. It accumulates
        NumPy errors/counts with the same mask/metric definitions. It does not refit the
        table using validation observations.
        
        These functions are baseline-specific CPU evaluators, not one universal neural
        API. Small LSTM validation lives in train_lstm.py; contextual train/validation
        lives in train_context_lstm.py. They share the same original-unit metric rules.
        
        ## Important distinction
        
        Loss averages one batch for gradients. Reporting must pool all included targets,
        not average batch means without weights. The last partial batch and different
        zero coverage make that distinction observable. Mask before percentage division.
        
        See [formulas and aggregation](../concepts/09_metrics_and_aggregation.md).
        ''',
        'lstm_model.md':'''# Implementation: lstm_model.py
        
        Source: [lstm_model.py](../../lstm_model.py). Class: `TrafficLSTM`.
        
        This original traffic-only reference uses one LSTM layer with hidden width 32
        and a linear head producing 12 steps. It has 4,876 trainable parameters and no
        calendar, sensor embedding, or spatial interactions.
        
        ## Construction
        
        Validate dimensions and scale, register fixed float32 mean/std buffers, create
        `nn.LSTM(1,32,num_layers=1,batch_first=True)`, and `nn.Linear(32,12)`.
        Buffers move with the model and appear in state_dict but are not optimizer weights.
        
        ## Forward path
        
        1. Validate input `(B,12,N,1)` and basic type/nonempty dimensions.
        2. Permute to `(B,N,12,1)` and reshape to `(B*N,12,1)`.
        3. Run LSTM with fresh default zero states.
        4. Select last-step hidden output `(B*N,32)`.
        5. Apply linear head `(B*N,12)`.
        6. Restore `(B,12,N,1)` and inverse-normalize.
        
        The output head is unconstrained; predictions are not clipped to nonnegative
        values in current training/evaluation. Adding clipping would change the method
        and should not be silently introduced after seeing test results.
        
        This model remains intact as an educational reference. ContextLSTM has a different
        architecture and checkpoint shape; its weights cannot be directly loaded here.
        
        See [LSTM mechanics](../concepts/10_lstm_gates_and_states.md) and
        [parameter counts](../concepts/16_parameter_counts_and_capacity.md).
        ''',
        'check_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: check_lstm.py
        
        Source: [check_lstm.py](../../check_lstm.py).
        
        This is a real-data CPU diagnostic, not training or evaluation of generalization.
        It sets seed 2023 and two CPU threads, fits the training scale, and loads the
        first four chronological training windows.
        
        ## Checks
        
        - Forward output matches target shape `(4,12,716,1)` and is finite.
        - Masked MAE backward reaches every trainable parameter tensor with finite,
          nonzero gradients.
        - Parameter values remain exactly unchanged because no optimizer step is called.
        - Fixed mean/std buffers do not receive gradients.
        - Individual selected sensor calls match their batched positions within tolerance.
        - Changing one sensor does not affect other sensors' forecasts.
        - Repeated calls use fresh states, and a batch of one works.
        
        ```bash
        python check_lstm.py
        ```
        
        Observed initial first-batch MAE was 193.0234. Random initialized predictions
        are not evidence of model quality. Another diagnostic can have a different
        initial score even with the same seed when construction/iterator order differs,
        because those operations consume RNG state.
        
        No artifacts, checkpoints, or test scores are created. These checks support

        See [the model](lstm_model.md) and [the update diagnostic](train_lstm_diagnostic.md).
        ''',
         'train_lstm_diagnostic.md':'''# Implementation: train_lstm_diagnostic.py
        
        Source: [train_lstm_diagnostic.py](../../train_lstm_diagnostic.py).
        
        This adds actual Adam updates to the small LSTM check. It starts fresh and runs

        Seed 2023 and a separate shuffle generator define training-window order.
        
        ## Flow
        
        Load training data and scaler, build TrafficLSTM/Adam, and record initial weights.
        Measure a fixed first-four-window training probe before updates. For each shuffled
        batch: skip an empty mask; zero gradients; forward; masked MAE; backward;
        check gradients; Adam step; check finite weights; print the pre-update batch loss.

        parameter tensors changed and no batches were skipped. Pooled diagnostic

         'train_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: train_lstm.py
        
        Source: [train_lstm.py](../../train_lstm.py).
        
        This original script starts one fresh CPU epoch, not 50 epochs or resume. It

        ## Functions

         'continue_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: continue_lstm.py
        
        Source: [continue_lstm.py](../../continue_lstm.py).
        
        This continues the original small LSTM/Adam run to a chosen total epoch count.
        It is not the contextual suite trainer. Original protocol remains historical
        provenance; the actual continuation execution device is recorded separately.
        
        ## Functions and lifecycle
        
        - `restore_training`: reconstruct model, restore weights, place on selected device,

        - `device_batches` / `validate_device`: move x/y/mask consistently for scoring.
        - `metrics_match`: coverage exact, floating metrics within rtol 1e-5/atol 1e-4
          to handle CPU/CUDA differences.
        - `train_epoch`: all training windows, empty-mask skips, checks, original-unit loss.
        - `save_checkpoint` / `save_report`: temporary writes followed by replacement.

          continue and save best/last/history reports.
        
        The check-only mode performs full frozen validation AND one disposable Adam

        'evaluate_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: evaluate_lstm.py
        
        Source: [evaluate_lstm.py](../../evaluate_lstm.py).
        
        This evaluates the original traffic-only LSTM checkpoint, not ContextLSTM.
        Default input is runs/lstm_50epochs_gpu_v1/best.pt. Existing output directories
        are preserved rather than overwritten.
        
        ## Preconditions
        
        Confirm checkpoint epoch/validation match the completed training report. Verify
        original source hashes, dataset hash, chronological boundaries and train-only
        normalization. Reconstruct TrafficLSTM, load strictly, and recheck full validation
        on the evaluation device before allowing test scoring.
        
        ## score_test
        
        Sets eval/no-grad, predicts sequential test batches, and accumulates errors and
        counts separately for each of 12 horizons in float64. Overall RMSE comes from
        all squared errors, not averaging horizon RMSE. Independently count each lead's
        source nonzero targets. Assert all model-state tensors and checkpoint bytes
        remain unchanged, and that no parameter gradients were created.
        
        ## Executed result
        
        CPU evaluation of epoch 49 covered 6,997 test windows and 58,158,396 valid pairs:
        MAE 39.7079, RMSE 62.9506, MAPE 27.4996%. Lead MAE rose from 15.3701 at assumed
        15 minutes to 62.9966 at 180 minutes. The test pass took about 10.09 seconds,
        including loading/batching/metrics; it is not isolated GPU inference latency.
        
        [The report](../../reports/lstm_test_v1.md) contains all lead results and limits.
        Synthetic examples checked masked overall/per-lead metrics and partial batches.
        No additional training or optimizer was used. These observed test scores must
        not be used for checkpoint selection or represented as newly unseen afterward.
        
        Contextual evaluation remains separate future work; checkpoint schemas differ.
        ''',
        'context_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: context_lstm.py
        
        Source: [context_lstm.py](../../context_lstm.py). Class: ContextLSTM.
        
        This is one configurable architecture with hidden widths 128/256/384, two layers,
        no dropout, and a direct 12-step head. It adds historical calendar and sensor
        identity to the traffic-only reference.
        
        ## Modules and shapes
        
        Slot embedding `(96,16)`, weekday embedding `(7,8)`, and sensor embedding
        `(716,16)` concatenate with traffic to form 41 inputs per historical step.
        
        ```text
        x:                              (B,12,N,1)
        calendar:                       (B,12,2)
        expanded calendar/sensor data:   (B,12,N,40)
        combined features:              (B,12,N,41)
        reordered LSTM sequences:        (B*N,12,41)
        top-layer final hidden:         (B*N,H)
        linear head:                    (B*N,12)
        restored original-unit output:  (B,12,N,1)
        ```
        
        The recurrent output at the last input time is used, not a future target.
        `input_calendar(target_starts,history)` builds the historical positions only.
        
        Optional `sensor_ids` enables isolated-sensor diagnostic calls while preserving
        that sensor's original embedding row. Normal training omits it and requires all
        716 sensors in original order. All states start fresh per window. Identity does
        not introduce traffic communication between sensors.
        
        Dimensions, calendar dtype/shape and basic device compatibility are checked.
        Embedding lookups enforce index bounds. Models are not automatically robust to
        arbitrary malformed external arrays; the data pipeline/audit define the contract.
        
        Exact parameter counts are 234,244 / 848,644 / 1,856,260. These are fresh models,
        not expanded/reused small-LSTM checkpoints.
        
        See [embeddings](../concepts/11_embeddings_and_context.md) and
        [GPU probe](check_context_lstm.md).
        ''',
        'check_context_lstm.md':'''# Implementation: check_context_lstm.py
        
        Source: [check_context_lstm.py](../../check_context_lstm.py).

        Weights are discarded at the end; no checkpoint/validation/test score is created.
        
        ## What is checked
        
        - Correct prediction shape and finite masked loss, gradients and weights.
        - A recurrent forward pre-hook captures actual LSTM input sequences.
        - Selected traffic, calendar embedding and sensor embedding positions match
          intended sources with zero tolerance, detecting axis/identity mistakes.
        - Isolated-sensor predictions match batched positions within stated tolerance.
        - Changing one input sensor leaves all other sensor predictions unchanged.

        Synchronize CUDA around updates, record mean timed-step duration and peak allocated/

        previous host parity failure in the rerun without loosening output tolerance.
        Actual cause was not conclusively isolated.

        See [precision/timing](../concepts/15_gpu_precision_and_timing.md).
        ''',

        | Window/example | One paired historical input and future target |
        | Batch | Up to four examples processed together |
        | Epoch | One full pass through eligible training examples |

        | Parameter | Learned weight or bias |
        | Buffer | Fixed model-associated state such as scaler statistics |

        | Cell state | LSTM internal memory updated by gates |
        | Loss | Training objective; original-unit masked MAE here |
        | Gradient | Derivative used to adjust a parameter |
        | Adam state | Running optimizer moments and step information |
        | Mask | Boolean inclusion flags; nonzero targets included |
        | Coverage | Number/fraction of included targets, not proven source validity |
        | Validation | Later data used to select settings/checkpoints |
        | Test | Frozen-system assessment after choices are fixed |

        root=Path('docs'); pages=sorted(root.rglob('*.md'))

    # Project documentation: learn the concepts, then follow the code
    
    This folder explains the current traffic forecasting project as implemented,
    including the original small LSTM, its test evaluation, and the stronger
    contextual LSTM capacity experiment. It is a learning reference, not a claim that
    all planned experiments are finished.
    
    ## Start here
    
    1. Read [project overview](project_overview.md) for the goal and architecture.
    2. Read the concept guides in order below, using the matching implementation
       walkthrough when you want to connect an idea to Python.
    3. Use [commands](commands.md) to inspect, check, start, pause or resume work.
    4. Read [results and status](results_and_status.md) for the dated observed snapshot.
    5. Read [PatchSTG reference](patchstg_reference.md) before interpreting comparisons.

    # Reading guide: understand the full traffic forecasting project
    
    Start here if you want to understand what we built, why each part exists, and
    how the pieces connect. Follow the stages in order rather than starting with
    the longest training script.
    
    The project compares traffic forecasting methods on processed SD data. We began
    with simple baselines, built a small LSTM, and then added contextual inputs and
    three predefined LSTM capacities. PatchSTG is currently a reference implementation
    and trained result in the previous project; it has not been rebuilt here.
    
    ## How to use this guide
    
    For each stage:
    
    1. Read the concept explanation.
    2. Read the implementation walkthrough.
    3. Open the linked Python file and trace the named functions.
    4. Answer the checkpoint questions in your own words before moving on.
    
    Keep [the glossary](docs/glossary.md) open. The [documentation index](docs/README.md)
    lists every topic and Python walkthrough. You do not need to memorize every line;
    aim to explain each function's inputs, outputs, and purpose.
    
    Reading does not require rerunning training. In particular, do not start another
    suite while one is already running. Existing result files are enough for the
    exercises below. Avoid editing training source during the current experiment:
    resume checks compare its recorded hashes.
    
    ## Stage 1 — Understand the question and the project map
    
    Read:
    
    - [Project overview](docs/project_overview.md).
    - [Forecasting problem](docs/concepts/01_forecasting_problem.md).
    
    Draw this pipeline on paper:
    
    ```text
    Traffic data → split → normalize inputs → windows → batches
                                                       ↓
                                                    predictor
                                                       ↓
                                  original-unit predictions versus targets
                                                       ↓
                                     training loss or evaluation metrics
    ```
    
    Keep the three experiments distinct: the original small LSTM, the new contextual
    LSTM capacity study, and the previous PatchSTG adaptation. Their results and
    checkpoint formats are not interchangeable.
    
    **Checkpoint:** What are we predicting? What do 12 history steps and 12 forecast
    steps mean? Which models were implemented in this folder? Why is BigST deferred?

    - [Audit implementation](docs/implementations/audit_data.md).
    - [Audit report and figures](reports/data_audit_v1/README.md).
    
    Open [audit_data.py](audit_data.py). Follow `audit_values`, `audit_metadata`, and
    `plot_patterns`. Then find `load_traffic` in [data_pipeline.py](data_pipeline.py).
    
    Write the meaning of each axis in `(35040,716,1)`. Explain these selections:
    
    ```python
    traffic[0, 0, 0]
    traffic[:12, 0, 0]
    traffic[0, :, 0]
    ```
    
    Look at the figures: describe daily changes and differences between sensors
    without inventing a cause for an abrupt drop or an all-zero interval.
    
    **Checkpoint:** What does an SHA-256 match establish? Does a zero necessarily
    mean missing data? What do we assume about timestamps and metadata ordering?
    Why is ID2 not a direct index into the 716-sensor array?

    """Evaluate a validation-selected frozen LSTM once, including each forecast lead."""
    
    import argparse
    import json
    import os
    import platform
    import time
    from pathlib import Path
    
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
    
    from continue_lstm import metrics_match, validate_device
    from data_pipeline import TrafficDataset, fit_normalization, load_traffic, split_boundaries
    from lstm_model import TrafficLSTM
    from train_lstm import sha256
    
    
    def score_test(model, loader, horizon):
        """Pool errors by horizon; do not average batch scores or per-lead RMSEs."""
        sums = np.zeros((3, horizon), dtype=np.float64)
        counts = np.zeros(horizon, dtype=np.int64)
        windows = 0
        device = next(model.parameters()).device
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            for batch in loader:
                prediction = model(batch["x"].to(device)).cpu().double().numpy()
                targets = batch["y"].double().numpy()
                masks = batch["target_mask"].numpy()
                if prediction.shape != targets.shape or not np.isfinite(prediction).all():
                    raise ValueError("Invalid test predictions.")
                for lead in range(horizon):
                    mask = masks[:, lead]
                    target = targets[:, lead][mask]
                    errors = np.abs(prediction[:, lead][mask] - target)
                    sums[:, lead] += [errors.sum(), np.square(errors).sum(),
                                      (errors / np.abs(target)).sum()]
                    counts[lead] += len(target)
                windows += len(targets)
    
        def metrics(total, count):
            if count == 0:
                raise ValueError("No included test targets.")
            return {"mae": float(total[0] / count), "rmse": float(np.sqrt(total[1] / count)),
                    "mape_percent": float(100 * total[2] / count), "valid_targets": int(count)}
    
        per_horizon = [dict(lead=i + 1, assumed_minutes=(i + 1) * 15,
                            **metrics(sums[:, i], counts[i])) for i in range(horizon)]
        return {"overall": metrics(sums.sum(axis=1), counts.sum()),
                "per_horizon": per_horizon, "windows": windows}
    
    
    def main():
        root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
        parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
        parser.add_argument("--checkpoint", type=Path, default=root / "runs/lstm_50epochs_gpu_v1/best.pt")
        parser.add_argument("--output-dir", type=Path, default=root / "runs/lstm_test_v1")
        parser.add_argument("--device", choices=("cpu", "cuda"), default="cpu")
        args = parser.parse_args()
        if args.output_dir.exists():
            raise FileExistsError("Choose a new output directory; existing evaluations are preserved.")
        os.environ.setdefault("CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG", ":4096:8")
        if args.device == "cuda" and not torch.cuda.is_available():
            raise RuntimeError("Requested CUDA is unavailable.")
        torch.set_num_threads(2)
        torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)
        checkpoint_hash = sha256(args.checkpoint)
        checkpoint = torch.load(args.checkpoint, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
        # Confirm this is the best checkpoint of the completed training run.
        training_report = json.loads((args.checkpoint.parent / "report.json").read_text())
        if (training_report["status"] != "complete"
                or checkpoint["epoch"] != training_report["best_epoch"]
                or checkpoint["validation"] != training_report["best_validation"]):
            raise ValueError("Checkpoint is not the completed run's validation-selected best.")
        provenance = checkpoint["provenance"]
        for name, expected in provenance["source_sha256"].items():
            if sha256(root / name) != expected:
                raise ValueError(f"Training source changed: {name}")
        data_path = root / "data/raw/largest_sd/flowsd.npz"
        if sha256(data_path) != provenance["data_sha256"]:
            raise ValueError("Dataset differs from training.")
        traffic = load_traffic(data_path)
        train_end, test_start = split_boundaries(len(traffic))
        if provenance["splits"] != {"train": [0, train_end], "validation": [train_end, test_start]}:
            raise ValueError("Split boundaries differ from training.")
        mean, std = fit_normalization(traffic[:train_end])
        if provenance["scaler"] != {"mean": float(mean), "std": float(std)}:
            raise ValueError("Normalization differs from training.")
        config = provenance["config"]
        model = TrafficLSTM(mean, std, config["hidden_size"], config["history"], config["horizon"])
        model.load_state_dict(checkpoint["model_state"], strict=True)
        model.to(args.device)
        before = {name: value.detach().cpu().clone() for name, value in model.state_dict().items()}
        def loader(interval):
            dataset = TrafficDataset(traffic, interval, mean, std, config["history"], config["horizon"])
            return DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=config["batch_size"], shuffle=False, num_workers=0)
        validation = validate_device(model, loader((train_end, test_start)))
        if not metrics_match(validation, checkpoint["validation"]):
            raise ValueError("Evaluation-device validation differs from checkpoint beyond tolerance.")
        print(f"Epoch {checkpoint['epoch']} frozen; validation reproduced on {args.device}.", flush=True)
        args.output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = score_test(model, loader((test_start, len(traffic))), config["horizon"])
        seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
        if result["windows"] != 6997:
            raise ValueError("Incomplete test coverage.")
        # Independently count masks directly from source slices at each lead.
        starts = range(test_start, len(traffic) - config["horizon"] + 1)
        for lead, item in enumerate(result["per_horizon"]):
            expected = np.count_nonzero(traffic[starts.start + lead:starts.stop + lead])
            if expected != item["valid_targets"]:
                raise ValueError("Test target coverage mismatch.")
        for name, value in model.state_dict().items():
            torch.testing.assert_close(value.cpu(), before[name], rtol=0, atol=0)
        if any(p.grad is not None for p in model.parameters()) or sha256(args.checkpoint) != checkpoint_hash:
            raise RuntimeError("Frozen-state verification failed.")
        result.update(status="complete", selected_epoch=checkpoint["epoch"], device=args.device,
                      checkpoint=str(args.checkpoint.resolve()), checkpoint_sha256=checkpoint_hash,
                      checkpoint_unchanged=True, model_state_unchanged=True,
                      validation_recheck=validation, scoring_seconds=seconds,
                      test_target_interval=[test_start, len(traffic)], batch_size=config["batch_size"],
                      python=platform.python_version(), torch=str(torch.__version__),
                      evaluation_source_sha256=sha256(Path(__file__).resolve()),
                      device_helpers_sha256=sha256(root / "continue_lstm.py"), provenance=provenance)
        (args.output_dir / "report.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
        print(json.dumps({"epoch": result["selected_epoch"], "windows": result["windows"],
                          "test": result["overall"], "scoring_seconds": seconds}, indent=2), flush=True)
        print("No optimizer, gradients or weight updates. Report:", args.output_dir / "report.json")
    
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()

    """Freeze the completed 128/256 search, evaluate the winner, and build the report."""
    
    import argparse
    import json
    import math
    import time
    from datetime import datetime, timezone
    from pathlib import Path
    
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
    
    from context_lstm import ContextLSTM, input_calendar
    from data_pipeline import TrafficDataset, fit_normalization, load_traffic, split_boundaries
    from train_context_lstm import run_epoch, setup
    from train_lstm import sha256
    
    
    def select_completed(suite, root):
        """Use validation only; 384 is deliberately outside the revised search."""
        candidates = []
        for width in (128, 256):
            directory = suite / f"hidden_{width}"
            report = json.loads((directory / "report.json").read_text())
            if report["status"] != "complete" or [e["epoch"] for e in report["epochs"]] != list(range(1, 51)):
                raise ValueError(f"Width {width} is not a completed 50-epoch run.")
            best_row = min(report["epochs"], key=lambda e: e["validation"]["mae"])
            if best_row["epoch"] != report["best_epoch"] or best_row["validation"] != report["best_validation"]:
                raise ValueError("Training report selection is inconsistent.")
            path = directory / "best.pt"
            checkpoint = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
            if (checkpoint["hidden_size"] != width or checkpoint["epoch"] != report["best_epoch"]
                    or checkpoint["validation"] != report["best_validation"]):
                raise ValueError("Best checkpoint disagrees with training report.")
            for epoch in report["epochs"]:
                if (epoch["training"]["windows"] != 21001
                        or epoch["validation"]["windows"] != 6997
                        or epoch["validation"]["valid_targets"] != 58367674):
                    raise ValueError("Unexpected training/validation coverage.")
            for name, expected in checkpoint["metadata"]["source_sha256"].items():
                if sha256(root / name) != expected:
                    raise ValueError(f"Original training source changed: {name}")
            candidates.append({"hidden_size": width, "epoch": checkpoint["epoch"],
                               "validation": checkpoint["validation"],
                               "parameters": report["parameters"],
                               "checkpoint": str(path.resolve()), "checkpoint_sha256": sha256(path),
                               "training_report_sha256": sha256(directory / "report.json")})
        winner = min(candidates, key=lambda c: (c["validation"]["mae"], c["hidden_size"]))
        return {"selection_rule": "lowest best validation MAE among completed widths 128/256; smaller width on exact ties",
                "revised_scope": "User deferred width 384 for project completion before contextual test evaluation",
                "excluded_hidden_size": 384, "original_three_candidate_suite_complete": False,
                "candidates": candidates, "selected": winner,
                "frozen_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()}
    
    
    def metric_values(sums, count):
        if count == 0:
            return {"mae": None, "rmse": None, "mape_percent": None, "valid_targets": 0}
        return {"mae": float(sums[0] / count), "rmse": float(np.sqrt(sums[1] / count)),
                "mape_percent": float(100 * sums[2] / count), "valid_targets": int(count)}
    
    
    def score_frozen(model, loader):
        """Score horizons and sensors without training or storing all predictions."""
        horizon = model.horizon
        sensor_count = model.sensors
        lead_sums = np.zeros((3, horizon), dtype=np.float64)
        sensor_sums = np.zeros((3, sensor_count), dtype=np.float64)
        lead_counts = np.zeros(horizon, dtype=np.int64)
        sensor_counts = np.zeros(sensor_count, dtype=np.int64)
        windows = 0
        device = next(model.parameters()).device
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            for batch in loader:
                calendar = input_calendar(batch["target_start"].to(device), model.history)
                prediction = model(batch["x"].to(device), calendar).cpu().double().numpy()
                targets = batch["y"].double().numpy()
                mask = batch["target_mask"].numpy()
                if prediction.shape != targets.shape or not np.isfinite(prediction).all():
                    raise ValueError("Invalid frozen prediction.")
                error = np.abs(prediction - targets)
                absolute = np.where(mask, error, 0)
                squared = np.square(absolute)
                relative = np.divide(absolute, np.abs(targets), out=np.zeros_like(absolute), where=mask)
                for index, values in enumerate((absolute, squared, relative)):
                    lead_sums[index] += values.sum(axis=(0, 2, 3))
                    sensor_sums[index] += values.sum(axis=(0, 1, 3))
                lead_counts += mask.sum(axis=(0, 2, 3))
                sensor_counts += mask.sum(axis=(0, 1, 3))
                windows += len(targets)
                if windows % 1000 == 0:
                    print(f"  Test windows scored: {windows}/{len(loader.dataset)}", flush=True)
        if not lead_counts.sum() or windows != len(loader.dataset):
            raise ValueError("Incomplete or empty test evaluation.")
        return {"windows": windows, "overall": metric_values(lead_sums.sum(axis=1), lead_counts.sum()),
                "per_horizon": [dict(lead=i + 1, assumed_minutes=15 * (i + 1),
                                     **metric_values(lead_sums[:, i], lead_counts[i])) for i in range(horizon)],
                "per_sensor": [dict(sensor_index=i, **metric_values(sensor_sums[:, i], sensor_counts[i]))
                               for i in range(sensor_count)]}
    
    
    def check_reference(reference, current, data_hash, scaler):
        """Verify the old reported benchmark is on matching data, origins and masks."""
        if reference["source_hashes"]["flowsd.npz"] != data_hash or reference["scaler"] != scaler:
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG data/normalization does not match.")
        cfg = reference["config"]
        if (cfg["history"], cfg["horizon"], cfg["stride"]) != (12, 12, 1):
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG window protocol differs.")
        if cfg["splits"]["test"] != [28032, 35040]:
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG test boundaries differ.")
        recorded = reference["results"]["test"]
        if recorded["windows"] != current["windows"]:
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG test-window count differs.")
        if recorded["overall_pooled"]["valid_targets"] != current["overall"]["valid_targets"]:
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG mask coverage differs.")
        if [h["valid_targets"] for h in recorded["per_horizon"]] != [h["valid_targets"] for h in current["per_horizon"]]:
            raise ValueError("PatchSTG per-horizon mask coverage differs.")
    
    
    def build_comparison(output, selection, result, previous, root):
        """Use existing reference reports; never claim they were newly evaluated."""
        import matplotlib
        matplotlib.use("Agg")
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    
        files = {"Persistence": "persistence_sd_v1.json", "Seasonal average": "seasonal_average_sd_v1.json",
                 "PatchSTG adaptation (previous run)": "patchstg_sd_seed2023_test_v1.json"}
        refs = {label: json.loads((previous / "reports" / name).read_text()) for label, name in files.items()}
        patch = refs["PatchSTG adaptation (previous run)"]
        check_reference(patch, result, result["data_sha256"], result["scaler"])
        comparison = []
        for label, reference in refs.items():
            if reference["source_hashes"]["flowsd.npz"] != result["data_sha256"]:
                raise ValueError("Baseline data differs.")
            cfg = reference["config"]
            if (cfg["history"], cfg["horizon"], cfg["stride"]) != (12, 12, 1) or cfg["splits"]["test"] != [28032, 35040]:
                raise ValueError("Baseline test protocol differs.")
            test = reference["results"]["test"]
            if (test["windows"] != result["windows"]
                    or [h["valid_targets"] for h in test["per_horizon"]]
                    != [h["valid_targets"] for h in result["per_horizon"]]):
                raise ValueError("Reference target coverage differs.")
            comparison.append({"model": label, "test": test["overall_pooled"],
                               "source": str((previous / "reports" / files[label]).resolve()),
                               "source_sha256": sha256(previous / "reports" / files[label]),
                               "evaluation_origin": "historical measured report; not rerun here"})
        comparison.append({"model": "Contextual LSTM 256", "test": result["overall"],
                           "evaluation_origin": "new frozen evaluation in this project"})
        (output / "comparison.json").write_text(json.dumps(comparison, indent=2) + "\n")
    
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
        for candidate in selection["candidates"]:
            report = json.loads((Path(candidate["checkpoint"]).parent / "report.json").read_text())
            epochs = report["epochs"]
            width = candidate["hidden_size"]
            axes[0].plot([e["epoch"] for e in epochs], [e["training"]["mae"] for e in epochs], label=f"{width} train")
            axes[1].plot([e["epoch"] for e in epochs], [e["validation"]["mae"] for e in epochs], label=f"{width} validation")
            axes[1].scatter([candidate["epoch"]], [candidate["validation"]["mae"]])
        for axis, title in zip(axes, ("Training (weights evolve)", "Validation (fixed weights per epoch)")):

            axis.legend()
        fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(output / "learning_curves.png", dpi=150); plt.close(fig)
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
